entities.summary:
The semi-presidential system is a form of governance characterized by the coexistence of a president and a prime minister, each holding distinct powers within the executive branch. Emerging prominently in the latter half of the 20th century, this system has been adopted in various countries across the globe, with notable examples including France, Russia, and Portugal. The semi-presidential system matters significantly in the context of global governance as it reflects a compromise between presidential and parliamentary systems, allowing for a dual executive that can stabilize or destabilize political landscapes depending on the context. Key political figures such as Charles de Gaulle in France were instrumental in shaping the semi-presidential model, influencing the operational dynamics of the government.

The adoption of the semi-presidential system can be traced back to the French Constitution of 1958 under de Gaulle, who sought to create a robust executive authority to counterbalance parliamentary instability. This system was designed to facilitate efficient governance while maintaining democratic accountability, allowing for a president who could serve as a national figurehead and a prime minister who could manage day-to-day operations of government. Over time, countries like Russia embraced this model following the dissolution of the Soviet Union in the 1990s, further demonstrating its adaptability to different political contexts and fostering a complex interplay between various branches of government.
